name: Danish
family: Indo-European, Germanic, North Germanic, East Scandinavian
variety: Standard Danish (rigsdansk) as spoken in Copenhagen, the variety of the IPA illustration (Grønnum 1998)
sources: Grønnum, Nina (1998). Danish. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 28(1-2), 99-105.
Basbøll, Hans (2005). The Phonology of Danish. Oxford University Press.
Grønnum, Nina (2005). Fonetik og fonologi: Almen og dansk. 3rd edition. Copenhagen: Akademisk Forlag.
Fischer-Jørgensen, Eli (1989). Phonetic analysis of the stød in standard Danish. Phonetica 46, 1-59.

Fischer-Jørgensen, Eli (1972). Formant frequencies of long and short Danish vowels. In Firchow et al. (eds.), Studies for Einar Haugen. The Hague: Mouton. Also in Annual Report of the Institute of Phonetics, University of Copenhagen 6.
Grønnum, Nina and Basbøll, Hans (2001). Consonant length, stød and morae in Standard Danish. Phonetica 58, 230-253.
Grønnum, Nina (1992). The Groundworks of Danish Intonation: An Introduction. Copenhagen: Museum Tusculanum Press.
Thorsen, Nina (1978). An acoustical investigation of Danish intonation. Journal of Phonetics 6, 151-175.
Puggaard-Rode, Rasmus. Stop! Hey, what's that sound? The representation and realization of Danish stops. Doctoral dissertation, Leiden University (LOT dissertation series 631).

vowel_formants.speaker: mean of eight adult male speakers of Standard Danish born between 1905 and 1930, long vowels said in isolation

contrasts: stød versus no stød on syllables with a long vowel or with a short vowel plus sonorant: hund [hunˀ] 'dog' versus hun [hun] 'she', vend [vɛnˀ] versus ven [vɛn], mord versus mor, læser [ˈlɛːˀsɐ] 'reads' versus læser [ˈlɛːsɐ] 'reader', anden [ˈanˀən] 'the duck' versus anden [ˈanən] 'other'
four degrees of height among front unrounded vowels, /i e ɛ a/, three among front rounded and among back vowels, giving one of the largest vowel inventories known
long versus short vowels with little difference of quality (hvile [ˈviːlə] versus vilde [ˈvilə])
aspirated /p t k/ versus unaspirated /b d ɡ/ at the start of a syllable; both series are voiceless
schwa versus full vowels in unstressed syllables
allophony: /p t k/ are aspirated at the start of a syllable, and /t/ is affricated [tˢ]; after /s/ and outside the syllable onset only the unaspirated series occurs
/b d ɡ/ are voiceless unaspirated [b̥ d̥ ɡ̊]; voicing between vowels is rare

consonant weakening in the coda and between a full vowel and schwa: /d/ is the 'soft d' [ð], a velarised laminal alveolar approximant without friction (mad [mað], gade [ˈɡ̊æːðə]); /ɡ/ is [j] after front vowels, [w] after back vowels, or is lost (bage, bog [b̥ɔwˀ], pige [ˈpʰiːə]); /v/ is [w] (hav [hɑw], liv [liwˀ]); /b/ may be [w] (løbe)
/r/ is a uvular or pharyngeal approximant [ʁ] in the onset and a vocalic glide [ɐ̯] in the coda, or merges with the vowel (mor [moɐ̯], lærer [ˈlɛːɐ]); -er is [ɐ]
vowels next to /r/ are lowered and retracted: /a/ is [ɑ], /ɛ/ is [a]-like (ret, ræd), /ø œ/ are [œ ɶ] (grøn), /ɔ/ is [ɒ]
short /a/ is front [a] before coronals and zero, and back [ɑ] before labials and velars (man versus tak)
schwa assimilates to a neighbouring sonorant or vowel, giving syllabic consonants and long vowels (gade [ˈɡ̊æːð̩], spille [ˈsb̥el̩], manden [ˈmanˀn̩], pige [ˈpʰiːi])
/sj/ is alveolo-palatal [ɕ] (sjov); /j/ after aspirated stops is voiceless
/v/ in the onset is a weak approximant [ʋ]

stød is laryngealisation (creaky voice): the syllable starts with raised pitch and intensity, then amplitude and pitch drop sharply and the voice becomes irregular; in a long vowel this falls in the second part of the vowel, in a short vowel plus sonorant it falls in the sonorant; in emphatic speech it may be a full glottal closure
stød and stress are lost on a verb that forms one stress unit with a following object or particle (unit accentuation)
phonotactics: /p t k h/ occur only at the start of a syllable, [ð w ŋ ɐ̯] only after the vowel
onset clusters of up to three consonants, the first being /s/ (spr, str, skr, spl)
stød needs a stressed syllable with stød basis: a long vowel, or a short vowel followed by a sonorant

stød is in general absent from words of two syllables ending in schwa (the old accent 2 words) and present in old monosyllables, also when the definite article is added (hus [huːˀs], huset [ˈhuːˀsəð])
unstressed syllables have [ə], [ɐ] or a syllabic consonant

stress.rule: Native words stress the first syllable of the stem, the prefixes be-, ge-, for- and er- are unstressed, and loans often stress the last or second-last syllable (student, universitet, station).
stress.cues: the pitch pattern of the stress group (a low stressed syllable followed by a high post-tonic syllable), duration and full vowel quality; intensity is a weak cue

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong: unstressed syllables have schwa or [ɐ], and schwa is commonly assimilated or dropped
rhythm.notes: Grønnum describes little or no final lengthening in Danish.

length.notes: Long and short vowels contrast with little difference of quality. Consonants are not contrastively long, but schwa assimilation produces long and syllabic sonorants. Vowels with stød are somewhat shorter than long vowels without it.

intonation.declarative: the stressed syllables of the successive stress groups lie on a line that falls steadily from the first to the last; there is no special nuclear accent and no final pitch movement
intonation.yes_no_question: a question with no mark of word order or question word has a level line through the stressed syllables; a question with inversion has a moderately falling line; a final rise is not required
intonation.wh_question: moderately falling line, less steep than in a statement
intonation.continuation: non-final clauses have a slope between those of the statement and the unmarked question
intonation.accent_shape: in Copenhagen each stress group has a low stressed syllable, a rise to a peak on the first unstressed syllable after it, and a gradual fall over the remaining unstressed syllables
intonation.notes: After Thorsen (1978) and Grønnum (1992, 1998): sentence type is signalled by the overall slope, not by a nuclear tone or a boundary tone. Regional varieties differ in the shape of the stress group pattern.

inventory.name: stød
inventory.description: laryngeal syllable accent on a stressed syllable with a long vowel or a short vowel plus sonorant: high pitch and intensity at the start, then a sharp drop of intensity and pitch with irregular vibration
inventory.duration: a long vowel with stød is a little shorter than one without

inventory.name: no stød
inventory.description: plain stressed syllable with the pitch of the stress group pattern

sandhi: stød is lost together with stress in unit accentuation and in the first part of many compounds
tone.notes: Danish has no lexical pitch contrast. Stød is listed here because it is the Danish counterpart of the Scandinavian word accents (stød words correspond to accent 1) and works as a lexical and grammatical contrast.

phonation: stød: creaky voice or laryngealisation as a contrastive property of syllables
aspiration of /p t k/ with affrication of /t/

problems: stød is not modelled: hun and hund, ven and vend, and the noun and the verb læser come out the same; the phoneme names that begin with '?' mark short vowels, and the IPA trace prints them with a glottal stop [ʔ] before the vowel that is neither spoken nor correct
/b d ɡ/ come from the base table and are voiced stops; Danish has voiceless unaspirated stops; /t/ is a plain aspirated stop without affrication
soft d uses the English dental fricative phoneme [ð] where Danish has a velarised alveolar approximant without friction
vowel length is not part of the phoneme string: it is set by context procedures (LongVowelLength, ShortVowelLength) and by the spelling rules, and the IPA trace never shows length
schwa is always pronounced: there is no schwa assimilation and there are no syllabic consonants (gade, spille, manden keep [ə])

stressed syllables carry the pitch peaks as in the other eSpeak languages; the Copenhagen pattern of a low stressed syllable and a high post-tonic syllable is not modelled, although the voice has its own tunes (s2, c2, q2, e2)
some vowel qualities are off: the long vowel of løbe and købe is the open [œ] instead of [øː]
questions are given the same tune whether they are yes-no or wh-questions
good: consonant weakening follows the language: soft d (mad, gade), [j] and [w] or loss for g (bage, bog, pige), [w] for v after a vowel (hav, liv, navn)
onset r is uvular [ʁ] and coda r is the glide [ɐ̯]; -er is an open central vowel
v in the onset is the approximant [ʋ]
a large rule file with many word-specific rules, and a pronunciation list of about 11,000 entries
statement, comma and question tunes were designed for Danish, with a small final movement

notes: The consonant list is phonetic: [b̥ d̥ ɡ̊] are the phonemes /b d ɡ/, and [ð w ɐ̯] are the weakened forms of /d/, /v ɡ/ and /r/. The vowel list follows Grønnum (1998); phonemic analyses count fewer vowels because several qualities are conditioned by /r/. The formant values belong to conservative speakers; Fischer-Jørgensen's phonemic /aː/ is the vowel now written [æː], and the vowels of present-day Copenhagen speech are closer still. I give no voice onset time values because I cannot quote the published figures with confidence.
